Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

vignette: Maya, a 46-year-old musician from New Zealand, found herself grappling with the aftermath of a life-threatening illness that had turned her world upside down. It had begun a year earlier when she was diagnosed with a severe respiratory condition. The diagnosis came as a shock, disrupting not only her health but the very essence of her identity as a performer. As she lay in the hospital bed, the sterile smell of antiseptic filled her nostrils, and she could hear the rhythmic beeping of machines that felt like a countdown to her own mortality. In those moments, she had experienced breathlessness that struck her like a bolt of lightning, filling her with an overwhelming sense of terror. The memories of that hospital stay were now inescapable triggers; even the faintest whiff of hospital disinfectant would send her spiraling back to those harrowing days, where each breath felt like a battle. In the months that followed her discharge, Maya's life became dominated by a constant undercurrent of anxiety. This pervasive threat only deepened her negative self-assessment, leading her to believe that she was incapable of handling the world around her, reinforcing her feelings of inadequacy and vulnerability. This pervasive sense of threat shaped her perception of reality, making her believe that every situation held the potential for danger, which in turn led her to withdraw from the world around her. She had tried to cope with her fears by avoiding anything related to medical cues. The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages - each new reminder confirmed what her body already believed about her vulnerability. With her senses heightened by this ongoing threat, even the faintest sound or sight could trigger memories of her illness, turning her surroundings into a minefield of reminders that she could not escape. The pervasive sense of danger she carried made ordinary cues feel like threats, and any reminder of her past illness became an inescapable trigger that sent her spiraling back into those moments of trauma. Hospitals, ambulances, or even discussions about health were now off-limits. She would cancel routine check-ups and steer clear of any situation that might remind her of the vulnerability she felt while fighting for breath. Yet, this avoidance only reinforced her sense of inadequacy. When the threat felt this close, avoiding any situation that could remind her of her trauma wasn't merely a strategy - it was the only rational thing to do. Maya had come to believe that managing her fear was beyond her capability, so avoiding anything that could trigger memories of her trauma felt not just logical but essential to her survival. This conviction made her avoidance feel like a necessary strategy; if she couldn't handle the fear, it was only logical to steer clear of anything that might trigger it, reinforcing her sense of helplessness. Maya's belief that she was inadequate and weak made her avoidance of medical situations feel not just rational, but essential; if she was truly defenseless, staying away from reminders of her trauma was the only way she could protect herself. Maya had come to believe that she was inadequate, unable to manage the fear that gripped her when faced with medical environments. This negative appraisal weighed heavily on her soul, translating into self-punishing thoughts that echoed in her mind. "I deserve to suffer because of what happened," she would tell herself, trapped in a cycle of counterfactual thinking where she endlessly replayed her illness and imagined how different her life could have been had she not faced such a dire health crisis. As time went on, Maya's nights became restless. She would wake up suddenly, heart racing, engulfed by the overwhelming need to check whether she was safe. The threat of her past loomed large, and her body reacted to danger before her mind could process it. Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading, and every small cue felt like a signal that danger was near. In this heightened state of alertness, even the most mundane situations felt charged with potential danger, which led her to avoid them altogether, further isolating her from the world. With the constant sense of danger lurking in her mind, it seemed only sensible to withdraw from situations that could provoke her anxiety, leading her to limit her world to places where she felt more secure. The looming threat made her strategies of avoidance feel not just prudent but necessary; if danger was everywhere, staying away from potential triggers was the only rational choice to protect herself. When every moment felt charged with the possibility of danger, it seemed only sensible to keep herself away from situations that could provoke her anxiety, leading her to withdraw from the world. This heightened state of alertness not only left her fatigued but also stirred self-doubt within her. "I can't trust that I will do the right thing," she thought often, questioning her ability to navigate her life now that it was fraught with uncertainty. It felt like a betrayal of her former self, a musician who thrived on emotional expression, now confined to a world of fear and doubt. This persistent feeling of danger convinced Maya that she was no longer the vibrant person she once was, solidifying her belief that she was now someone who could never feel safe or in control. The constant sense of threat she experienced daily only reinforced her negative self-assessment, whispering to her that this fear was evidence of her inadequacy and inability to cope with life as it once was. This ongoing threat also confirmed her belief that she was now fundamentally flawed, as the fear she felt underscored her conviction that she was no longer capable of managing her life. Maya's daily life began to shrink around her. The vibrant social events she once relished turned into daunting challenges as she felt trapped within a limited number of safe spaces. Her husband, noticing her withdrawal, encouraged her to engage with her music, but she would often make excuses, fearing that performing could rekindle the breathlessness that haunted her. Each time she hesitated to step onto a stage, she felt the weight of her perceived inadequacy as a musician, a role she loved but now viewed through the lens of her trauma. It was during a quiet evening at home, amidst the familiar chords of her guitar, that Maya realized she could not continue this way. The longing to reconnect with her music and the people she loved began to outweigh the fear that had taken root in her life. She hesitated but ultimately found the courage to seek help, hoping to reclaim her identity and break free from the chains of her trauma. What frightened her the most was the uncertainty of whether she could ever feel safe again, but deep down, she hoped to rediscover her voice and the joy that music had once brought her. Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, further deepening her negative self-assessment. With each anxious thought, she began to see herself as fundamentally flawed, concluding that if she was always on high alert, it was proof that she would never be capable of living a normal life again.

vignette_attempts.vignette: Maya, a 46-year-old musician from New Zealand, found herself grappling with the aftermath of a life-threatening illness that had turned her world upside down. It had begun a year earlier when she was diagnosed with a severe respiratory condition. The diagnosis came as a shock, disrupting not only her health but the very essence of her identity as a performer. As she lay in the hospital bed, the sterile smell of antiseptic filled her nostrils, and she could hear the rhythmic beeping of machines that felt like a countdown to her own mortality. In those moments, she had experienced breathlessness that struck her like a bolt of lightning, filling her with an overwhelming sense of terror. The memories of that hospital stay were now inescapable triggers; even the faintest whiff of hospital disinfectant would send her spiraling back to those harrowing days, where each breath felt like a battle. In the months that followed her discharge, Maya’s life became dominated by a constant undercurrent of anxiety. This pervasive sense of threat shaped her perception of reality, making her believe that every situation held the potential for danger, which in turn led her to withdraw from the world around her. She had tried to cope with her fears by avoiding anything related to medical cues. The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each new reminder confirmed what her body already believed about her vulnerability. With her senses heightened by this ongoing threat, even the faintest sound or sight could trigger memories of her illness, turning her surroundings into a minefield of reminders that she could not escape. Hospitals, ambulances, or even discussions about health were now off-limits. She would cancel routine check-ups and steer clear of any situation that might remind her of the vulnerability she felt while fighting for breath. Yet, this avoidance only reinforced her sense of inadequacy. When the threat felt this close, avoiding any situation that could remind her of her trauma wasn't merely a strategy — it was the only rational thing to do. Maya had come to believe that managing her fear was beyond her capability, so avoiding anything that could trigger memories of her trauma felt not just logical but essential to her survival. This conviction made her avoidance feel like a necessary strategy; if she couldn’t handle the fear, it was only logical to steer clear of anything that might trigger it, reinforcing her sense of helplessness. Maya's belief that she was inadequate and weak made her avoidance of medical situations feel not just rational, but essential; if she was truly defenseless, staying away from reminders of her trauma was the only way she could protect herself. Maya had come to believe that she was inadequate, unable to manage the fear that gripped her when faced with medical environments. This negative appraisal weighed heavily on her soul, translating into self-punishing thoughts that echoed in her mind. "I deserve to suffer because of what happened," she would tell herself, trapped in a cycle of counterfactual thinking where she endlessly replayed her illness and imagined how different her life could have been had she not faced such a dire health crisis. As time went on, Maya’s nights became restless. She would wake up suddenly, heart racing, engulfed by the overwhelming need to check whether she was safe. The threat of her past loomed large, and her body reacted to danger before her mind could process it. Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading, and every small cue felt like a signal that danger was near. In this heightened state of alertness, even the most mundane situations felt charged with potential danger, which led her to avoid them altogether, further isolating her from the world. With the constant sense of danger lurking in her mind, it seemed only sensible to withdraw from situations that could provoke her anxiety, leading her to limit her world to places where she felt more secure. When every moment felt charged with the possibility of danger, it seemed only sensible to keep herself away from situations that could provoke her anxiety, leading her to withdraw from the world. This heightened state of alertness not only left her fatigued but also stirred self-doubt within her. "I can't trust that I will do the right thing," she thought often, questioning her ability to navigate her life now that it was fraught with uncertainty. It felt like a betrayal of her former self, a musician who thrived on emotional expression, now confined to a world of fear and doubt. This persistent feeling of danger convinced Maya that she was no longer the vibrant person she once was, solidifying her belief that she was now someone who could never feel safe or in control. The constant sense of threat she experienced daily only reinforced her negative self-assessment, whispering to her that this fear was evidence of her inadequacy and inability to cope with life as it once was. Maya's daily life began to shrink around her. The vibrant social events she once relished turned into daunting challenges as she felt trapped within a limited number of safe spaces. Her husband, noticing her withdrawal, encouraged her to engage with her music, but she would often make excuses, fearing that performing could rekindle the breathlessness that haunted her. Each time she hesitated to step onto a stage, she felt the weight of her perceived inadequacy as a musician, a role she loved but now viewed through the lens of her trauma. It was during a quiet evening at home, amidst the familiar chords of her guitar, that Maya realized she could not continue this way. The longing to reconnect with her music and the people she loved began to outweigh the fear that had taken root in her life. She hesitated but ultimately found the courage to seek help, hoping to reclaim her identity and break free from the chains of her trauma. What frightened her the most was the uncertainty of whether she could ever feel safe again, but deep down, she hoped to rediscover her voice and the joy that music had once brought her. Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, further deepening her negative self-assessment. With each anxious thought, she began to see herself as fundamentally flawed, concluding that if she was always on high alert, it was proof that she would never be capable of living a normal life again.
